newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Church brokers Central Africa Republic peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Church brokers Central Africa Republic peace talks.

text.p: The government and mutinous soldiers in Central African Republic began peace talks in the capital Bangui on Saturday, with the Roman Catholic Church mediating, political and military sources said.
Bangui's archbishop, Monsignor Joachim Ndayen, hosted the talks at his residence as part of efforts to defuse the crisis which began a week ago with the third army revolt this year.
Troops from former colonial power France, who intervened in May to put down a bloody revolt which threatened to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, provided security.

The capital was calm on Saturday with loyalists and French troops guarding strategic points in the city. The mutineers control the south of the city, the main fuel depot and the Kassai barracks. Fuel was scarce.
Patasse was visiting Europe. It was not immediately clear when he would return.

The two sides exchanged hostages late on Thursday. One report on Friday said the mutineers had subsequently taken hostage Enock Dernt Lakoue, head of the opposition Social Democratic Party and a man tipped by some as a potential successor to Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoumpande.

The army is divided between soldiers from Patasse's northern region and militants from the south, suspected of allegiance to former president Andre Kolingba, one of several candidates defeated by Patasse in multiparty elections in 1993.
Captain Anicet Saulet, who was leading the mutineers' delegation to the talks, issued a statement on Wednesday restating a major objective as the disarmament of civilian militias loyal to Patasse.

"The reason for the action of the military is to disarm the civilian militia and Codos (hired guns) of Chadian and Sudanese nationality. We will not lay down our arms until the completion of this mission," his statement said.
The mutineers have also demanded pay from 1992 and 1993 and for Patasse to revoke a decree ordering a regiment involved in the pay revolts in April and May to a base out of the capital.
They also want implementation of recommendations made by a national conference after the May revolt, including forming a professional army with a greater role in national life.
France has reinforced its Bangui base from Chad. The French contingent in Bangui now numbers 1,500 men.

French troops have so far confined their role to guarding the city centre, the presidential palace, the radio and television station and other strategic points. They clashed with rebel soldiers repeatedly during a mutiny in May.
Ngoumpande, appointed by Patasse as part of measures to defuse the more serious mutiny in May, said on Thursday that the latest revolt was political.
"This uprising, contrary to previous mutinies, was clearly politically motivated right from the start," he told heads of diplomatic missions in Bangui.
